questions.question: Which State launched India' first PPP green waste processing plant?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madhya Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Madhya Pradesh launched India’s first **Public-Private Partnership (PPP) based green waste processing plant**, a significant step towards sustainable waste management.
 
• Located in **Indore**, this plant was inaugurated to process wet and dry waste generated in the city efficiently.
 
• The plant operates on advanced waste segregation and recycling technologies to convert biodegradable waste into **bio-CNG**, a renewable energy source.
 
• The initiative is a key component of Indore’s consistent efforts to remain India’s cleanest city under the **Swachh Survekshan rankings** for several consecutive years.
 
• This innovative model integrates private sector participation in waste management, ensuring environmental sustainability and resource optimization.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chhattisgarh:**

 
 
• Chhattisgarh has emerged as a model for decentralized waste management systems, especially in rural areas.
 
• The state has implemented **solid waste management initiatives** through women-run self-help groups, focusing on segregation, composting, and recycling.
 
• It has also established **Garbage Clinic services** in urban areas to improve cleanliness and waste collection efficiency.
 
 
 
• **Kerala:**
 
 
• Kerala is recognized for its community-driven waste management programs and **plastic-free initiatives**.
 
• The state promotes decentralized composting and encourages households to manage biodegradable waste at the source.
 
• Projects like **Green Protocol** aim to minimize waste generation during public events and celebrations.
 
 
 
• **Telangana:**
 
 
• Telangana has implemented significant waste management reforms, particularly in urban areas like Hyderabad.
 
• The **Hyderabad Integrated Solid Waste Management (ISWM)** project focuses on waste segregation, transportation, and treatment.
 
• The state also promotes the establishment of waste-to-energy plants to convert municipal waste into electricity.

questions.question: This freedom fighter proclaimed himself the Peshwa during the Revolt of 1857 and gathered armed forces and expelled the British garrison from the city. He was the adopted son of the late Peshwa Baji Rao. The leader in question is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nana Saheb**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Nana Saheb** was a prominent leader during the Revolt of 1857 and played a crucial role in organizing the uprising against British rule.
 
• He was the adopted son of **Peshwa Baji Rao II**, the last Peshwa of the Maratha Empire.
 
• During the revolt, Nana Saheb proclaimed himself the **Peshwa** and led an armed resistance against the British forces.
 
• He expelled the British garrison from **Kanpur**, which became one of the centers of the rebellion.
 
• Nana Saheb’s leadership and military strategies were pivotal in the initial success of the rebellion in Kanpur, although the British later regained control of the city.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kunwar Singh**

 
 
• Kunwar Singh was one of the leading figures of the Revolt of 1857 and hailed from the state of Bihar.
 
• He was the **Raja of Jagdishpur** and led the uprising in Bihar against British forces.
 
• Despite being over 80 years old, Kunwar Singh displayed remarkable bravery and fought valiantly against the British.
 
• He is remembered for his guerrilla tactics and his ability to rally local forces against colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Mangal Pandey**
 
 
• Mangal Pandey was an Indian soldier in the British East India Company’s army who is often regarded as one of the first martyrs of the Revolt of 1857.
 
• He is best known for his attack on British officers at **Barrackpore**, which is considered to be one of the incidents that sparked the uprising.
 
• Mangal Pandey’s actions were driven by anger over the introduction of cartridges rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat, which offended both Hindu and Muslim sentiments.
 
• He was executed by the British, but his bravery inspired widespread resistance across India.
 
 
 
• **Tantia Tope**
 
 
• Tantia Tope was another prominent leader of the Revolt of 1857 and a close ally of Nana Saheb.
 
• He is best known for his military expertise and his role in organizing armed resistance against the British forces.
 
• After the fall of Kanpur, Tantia Tope carried on the rebellion by joining forces with Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi and other leaders.
 
• He used guerrilla warfare tactics to challenge British control but was eventually captured and executed in 1859.

• This vast expanse contributes to India having multiple time zones geographically, but the country follows a single standard time (Indian Standard Time, IST).

• The **north-south extent** of India (from Kashmir to Kanyakumari) is approximately 3214 kilometers.

questions.question: Which of the following devices performs optical character recognition (OCR)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**OCR Scanner**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **OCR Scanner** is a specialized device used for Optical Character Recognition (OCR), which converts printed or handwritten text into machine-readable text.
 
• It works by scanning the text and using advanced algorithms to recognize characters and symbols, converting them into editable digital formats such as Word or PDF.
 
• OCR technology is widely used in document digitization, enabling the extraction of data from forms, invoices, or books for digital archiving or processing.
 
• It eliminates the need for manual data entry and is instrumental in applications such as automated data processing, text retrieval, and e-discovery.
 
• Modern OCR systems are capable of recognizing multiple languages and complex font styles with high accuracy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **OMR Scanner**

 
 
• OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition, which is used to read marks made on pre-designed forms, such as multiple-choice answer sheets.
 
• Unlike OCR, OMR does not recognize text but detects the presence or absence of marks in specific areas.
 
• OMR scanners are commonly used in educational assessments, surveys, and voting systems.
 
 
 
• **Flatbed Scanner**
 
 
• A flatbed scanner is a general-purpose scanning device that captures high-resolution images of documents, photos, or other objects placed on its glass surface.
 
• It does not perform OCR by default but can be combined with OCR software to convert scanned images into text.
 
• Flatbed scanners are versatile and widely used in offices and homes for document digitization.
 
 
 
• **Barcode Reader**
 
 
• A barcode reader is a device used to scan and decode barcodes containing encoded information about products or items.
 
• It uses laser or imaging technology to read barcodes and convert the data into a usable format, typically for inventory management or point-of-sale systems.
 
• Barcode readers are not designed to recognize text or characters like OCR scanners.

questions.question: Which Article deals with the constitution of Municipalities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 243Q**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 243Q** of the Constitution of India deals with the constitution of Municipalities, providing a framework for urban local governance.
 
• It mandates the formation of three types of municipalities in every state: **Nagar Panchayat** (for areas in transition from rural to urban), **Municipal Council** (for smaller urban areas), and **Municipal Corporation** (for larger urban areas).
 
• Municipalities are empowered to carry out functions related to urban development, including planning, infrastructure, sanitation, and public amenities.
 
• This Article forms part of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which aimed to strengthen decentralized governance in urban areas.
 
• It ensures democratic representation in municipalities through elected representatives, promoting grassroots democracy and efficient urban administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 243W:**

 
 
• This Article specifies the powers, authority, and responsibilities of Municipalities.
 
• It empowers municipalities to prepare plans for economic development and social justice, along with the implementation of schemes related to 18 functional areas listed in the Twelfth Schedule.
 
• Key functions include urban planning, water supply, sanitation, public health, urban forestry, slum improvement, and poverty alleviation.
 
 
 
• **Article 243Z:**
 
 
• This Article focuses on the audit and accounts of municipalities.
 
• It ensures financial accountability by mandating regular audits of municipal accounts by the State Government or an authorized agency.
 
• The Article aims to enhance transparency and efficiency in the management of municipal resources.
 
 
 
• **Article 243P:**
 
 
• Article 243P provides definitions related to municipalities and urban governance.
 
• Key terms such as "district," "municipal area," and "population" are defined for clarity in the application of other provisions under Part IXA of the Constitution.
 
• This Article serves as the foundation for understanding the framework of municipal governance introduced by the 74th Amendment.

questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act added the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**First Amendment Act, 1951**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution of India through the **First Constitutional Amendment Act of 1951**.
 
• It was created to protect legislation related to land reforms and agrarian laws from being challenged in courts on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights.
 
• The main objective of the Ninth Schedule was to ensure social justice by implementing laws that aimed at equitable distribution of land.
 
• The addition of the Ninth Schedule was done by inserting Article 31B, which provides immunity to laws listed under the schedule from judicial review.
 
• The First Amendment Act of 1951 was introduced by the then Prime Minister **Jawaharlal Nehru** and passed by Parliament to safeguard certain laws under the agenda of promoting social welfare.
 
• The Ninth Schedule originally contained 13 laws when it was enacted, and additional laws have been added over time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Seventeenth Amendment Act, 1964:**

 
 
• This amendment further expanded the Ninth Schedule by including 44 additional laws related to land reforms.
 
• It also amended Article 31A of the Constitution to broaden the scope of agrarian reforms and ensure protection of such laws from judicial scrutiny.
 
 
 
• **Twenty-ninth Amendment Act, 1972:**
 
 
• This amendment included two Kerala Land Reform Acts in the Ninth Schedule.
 
• The aim was to ensure that these land reforms laws were implemented without legal challenges under fundamental rights.
 
 
 
• **Fourth Amendment Act, 1955:**
 
 
• This amendment dealt with property rights and aimed at limiting the right to compensation for property acquisition.
 
• It was not directly related to the addition of the Ninth Schedule but focused on addressing issues pertaining to property laws.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ninth Schedule Overview:**

 
 
• The Ninth Schedule is a unique provision under the Indian Constitution that protects certain laws from judicial review.
 
• Over time, debates have arisen about the scope of judicial review and the possibility of misuse of the Ninth Schedule.
 
• In the landmark judgment of **I.R. Coelho vs. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)**, the Supreme Court ruled that laws placed under the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, are open to judicial review if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution.

questions.question: What is the function of a diathermic wall in a thermodynamic system?

options.text: It allows the flow of only work.
It prevents the exchange of both matter and energy.
It allows the exchange of matter only.
It allows the flow of heat between systems.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It allows the flow of heat between systems.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A diathermic wall is a type of boundary in thermodynamics that **permits the transfer of heat** between two systems or between a system and its surroundings.
 
• It does not allow the exchange of matter between systems, ensuring that the systems remain physically separate.
 
• Diathermic walls are typically used in thermodynamic experiments to **study heat transfer** while isolating other forms of energy transfer, such as work.
 
• Heat transfer occurs because of the temperature difference between systems separated by a diathermic wall.
 
• The concept of diathermic walls is crucial in understanding **thermal equilibrium**, as heat flows until both systems reach the same temperature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Main Theme: Thermodynamic Walls**

 
 
• Thermodynamic walls are boundaries that separate systems and influence the type of interaction between them.
 
• They can be classified into different types, including **adiabatic walls** (prevent heat transfer), **diathermic walls** (allow heat transfer), and **rigid walls** (prevent work transfer).
 
• The study of these walls helps in understanding the exchange of energy in various thermodynamic processes.

questions.question: Which of the following, set up in June 1986, is responsible for the management of civil aerodromes and civil enclaves as well as for maintenance and operation of aeronautical communication systems at all the airports?

questions.question: The increase in Earth's average temperature due to trapped gases is called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Greenhouse Effect**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **greenhouse effect** is the process by which certain gases in Earth’s atmosphere trap heat, preventing it from escaping into space and leading to a rise in Earth's average temperature.
 
• These greenhouse gases include **carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapor, and fluorinated gases**, which act like a blanket surrounding the planet.
 
• Human activities, such as burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial processes, have significantly increased the concentration of these gases, exacerbating the greenhouse effect.
 
• The greenhouse effect is a natural phenomenon that is essential for maintaining the Earth’s temperature within a range suitable for life, but its intensification due to human activities is a major driver of **global warming**.
 
• This process is closely linked to **climate change**, which encompasses long-term changes in global or regional climate patterns caused by natural and anthropogenic factors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ocean Acidification:**

 
 
• Ocean acidification refers to the decrease in pH levels of the Earth’s oceans due to the absorption of excess carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere.
 
• It poses a major threat to marine ecosystems, particularly organisms that rely on calcium carbonate for their shells and skeletons, such as corals and shellfish.
 
• Ocean acidification is a direct consequence of increased greenhouse gas emissions but is distinct from the greenhouse effect.
 
 
 
• **Ozone Depletion:**
 
 
• Ozone depletion refers to the thinning of the ozone layer in the Earth’s stratosphere, primarily caused by the release of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances.
 
• The ozone layer protects life on Earth by absorbing harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.
 
• Unlike the greenhouse effect, ozone depletion does not directly contribute to global warming but has its own environmental consequences, such as increased UV radiation exposure.
 
 
 
• **Climate Change:**
 
 
• Climate change refers to significant changes in global or regional climate patterns over time, caused by natural factors, human activities, or both.
 
• The greenhouse effect plays a major role in driving climate change by contributing to global warming.
 
• Other manifestations of climate change include rising sea levels, melting glaciers, extreme weather events, and shifts in ecosystems.

questions.question: The commercialisation of agriculture under the British transformed the rural economy. What did 'commercialisation of agriculture' in British India lead to?

__
 
• Commercialisation of agriculture under British rule in India meant that agricultural practices were increasingly oriented towards market production rather than subsistence farming.
 
• This change was primarily driven by the colonial government's demand for raw materials, such as cotton, indigo, and jute, to fuel the Industrial Revolution in Britain.
 
• The focus shifted from growing food crops to cultivating cash crops, which were meant for export to Britain.
 
• Crops such as cotton, indigo, opium, tea, and jute became prominent, often replacing traditional food crops, leading to a decline in the food grain supply for local consumption.
 
• The increased production of cash crops disrupted traditional agrarian economies, leading to the dependency of Indian farmers on fluctuating global markets and exploitative colonial policies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Elimination of rural debt:**

 
 
• The commercialisation of agriculture under British rule did not lead to the elimination of rural debt. On the contrary, it often increased rural indebtedness.
 
• The growing dependence on moneylenders for credit to purchase seeds and pay taxes led many farmers into a cycle of debt.
 
• High taxation policies and fluctuating prices of cash crops further exacerbated this issue, leaving farmers vulnerable to exploitation.
 
 
 
• **Growth of self-sufficient villages:**
 
 
• Contrary to the suggestion, the commercialisation of agriculture eroded the self-sufficiency of Indian villages.
 
• Traditional practices, which focused on producing food grains for local consumption, were replaced by cash crop cultivation for export.
 
• This disrupted local agrarian economies and made villages dependent on external markets for their sustenance.
 
 
 
• **Rise in food grain production:**
 
 
• The commercialisation of agriculture did not lead to an increase in food grain production; in fact, it caused a decline in food production.
 
• Due to the prioritisation of cash crops like indigo, cotton, and tea, less land was available for cultivating essential food grains.
 
• This shift contributed to food shortages and famines in various parts of the country during British rule.

• In the case of Vihaan Kumar vs. State of Haryana, the Supreme Court declared the arrest illegal because the authorities failed to communicate the grounds of the arrest to the individual, violating their fundamental right under Article 22(1).
 
• This provision protects individuals against arbitrary arrests and ensures procedural fairness in criminal proceedings.
 
• The right to be informed of the grounds of arrest is essential for the effective exercise of the right to legal representation.
 
• The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of adhering to constitutional safeguards during the arrest to prevent the misuse of power by law enforcement agencies.

questions.question: How does the growth of tertiary activities reflect economic development in India?

options.text: It highlights a fall in manufacturing employment.
It indicates a slowdown in overall income generation.
It shows a shift back to farm-based occupations
It reflects improved services, urban growth and rising demand.

questions.solution:

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tertiary activities include services such as transport, communication, trade, health, education, and financial services.**
 
• **The growth of tertiary activities in India reflects urbanization, industrialization, and an increase in income levels, leading to higher demand for services.**
 
• **This growth indicates a structural shift in the economy from traditional agriculture and manufacturing to service-based industries.**
 
• **It also showcases advancements in technology and infrastructure that support urban growth and improved living standards.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (It highlights a fall in manufacturing employment):** While there may be shifts in employment from manufacturing to services, the growth of tertiary activities does not inherently indicate a decline in manufacturing employment. Instead, it shows diversification in employment opportunities.
 
• **Option 2 (It indicates a slowdown in overall income generation):** Tertiary sector growth is actually a sign of economic progress and increased income generation rather than a slowdown, as services contribute significantly to GDP and employment.
 
• **Option 3 (It shows a shift back to farm-based occupations):** The growth of tertiary activities is contrary to this idea, as it signifies a move away from agriculture toward modern services and urban-based professions.
 
• **Important Terms:**
 
 
• **Urbanization:** The process by which rural areas transform into urban centers due to migration and development.
 
• **Structural Shift:** A change in the dominant sectors of the economy, moving from primary (agriculture) to secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services).
 
• **Infrastructure Development:** Investments in transport, communication, and technology that support the growth of services and urbanization.
 
• **Income Growth:** Increased earnings for individuals and households, leading to higher consumption and demand for services.

questions.question: Which thermodynamic quantity helps determine the spontaneity of a chemical reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gibbs free energy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gibbs free energy (G) determines the **spontaneity** of a chemical reaction under constant pressure and temperature.
 
• A reaction is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs free energy, **ΔG, is negative**. This indicates that the system releases free energy.
 
• The formula for Gibbs free energy is ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, where:
 
 
• ΔH = change in enthalpy (heat energy)
 
• T = temperature in Kelvin
 
• ΔS = change in entropy
 
 
 
• **ΔG = 0** indicates a system in equilibrium, while ΔG > 0 means the reaction is non-spontaneous.
 
• Gibbs free energy is a critical thermodynamic quantity used in chemical, biological, and physical processes to predict reaction feasibility.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Enthalpy (ΔH):**

 
 
• Enthalpy is the total heat content of a system, often associated with the heat exchanged in a reaction under constant pressure.
 
• It is not sufficient on its own to predict reaction spontaneity, as it does not account for entropy changes.
 
• Reactions with a negative ΔH (exothermic) are often spontaneous, but this depends on the temperature and entropy.
 
 
 
• **Entropy (ΔS):**
 
 
• Entropy measures the disorder or randomness in a system.
 
• An increase in entropy (positive ΔS) favors spontaneity, as systems tend to move toward higher disorder.
 
• However, entropy alone cannot determine spontaneity; it must be considered alongside enthalpy and temperature.
 
 
 
• **Internal Energy:**
 
 
• Internal energy is the total energy contained within a system, including kinetic and potential energies of particles.
 
• It is a fundamental thermodynamic property but does not directly indicate reaction spontaneity.
 
 
 
• **Thermodynamic Spontaneity:**
 
 
• Spontaneity depends on the balance of enthalpy, entropy, and temperature, as captured in the Gibbs free energy equation.
 
• Understanding these interrelations is critical for predicting whether a chemical or physical process will occur naturally.

questions.question: Who is responsible for implementing the RTI Act in public departments?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Central Public Information Officer**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The RTI (Right to Information) Act, 2005 empowers citizens to seek information from public authorities to promote transparency and accountability.
 
• Under Section 5 of the RTI Act, every public authority is required to designate officers as Central Public Information Officers (CPIOs) or State Public Information Officers (SPIOs).
 
• CPIOs are responsible for receiving and responding to RTI applications and ensuring the requested information is provided within the stipulated time frame of 30 days.
 
• The CPIO is also responsible for transferring the application to the appropriate department if the information sought pertains to another public authority.
 
• In case of non-compliance or delay, the CPIO can be penalized, emphasizing their critical role in the implementation of the RTI Act.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Director General**

 
 
• The Director General is typically the head of specific organizations or departments such as police forces, military units, or scientific bodies, and is not directly responsible for RTI implementation.
 
• Their role involves overseeing operations, policies, and strategies within their domain but does not include managing RTI applications.
 
 
 
• **District Magistrate**
 
 
• The District Magistrate (DM) is primarily responsible for maintaining law and order in their jurisdiction and implementing developmental schemes.
 
• While DMs may play a supervisory role in ensuring transparency in district-level administration, they are not designated as information officers under the RTI Act.
 
 
 
• **Central Vigilance Officer**
 
 
• The Central Vigilance Officer (CVO) is tasked with overseeing vigilance activities within public organizations to prevent corruption.
 
• Their role focuses on maintaining integrity and accountability but does not encompass responding to RTI requests or ensuring transparency in public departments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **RTI Act:**

 
 
• The RTI Act, 2005, is a landmark legislation in India aimed at promoting transparency and accountability in governance.
 
• It empowers citizens to seek information from public authorities, thereby enabling them to participate in the democratic process more effectively.
 
• Public authorities are required to maintain records and provide them to applicants upon request unless exempted under Section 8 of the Act.
 
• The Act also establishes an appellate mechanism for individuals dissatisfied with the response received from Public Information Officers.

questions.question: Which of the following names is associated with the Faraizi Movement?

• His efforts were focused on mobilizing international support for India's independence, particularly from Germany and Turkey.

• It aimed at purifying Islamic practices and creating awareness about socio-economic injustices faced by Muslims under colonial rule.
 
• The movement opposed oppressive zamindari practices and British exploitation of farmers.
 
• Haji Shariatullah and his son Dudu Miyan were the key leaders of this movement, which influenced the socio-political landscape of Bengal.

questions.question: The McMahon Line is the boundary between India and which country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**China**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The McMahon Line is a boundary line between India and China, specifically between the northeastern Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh and Tibet (an autonomous region of China).
 
• It was drawn as part of the 1914 Simla Convention, an agreement between British India and Tibet, with China as a participant that ultimately did not accept the agreement.
 
• The McMahon Line spans approximately 890 kilometers and is considered the de facto boundary between India and China in the eastern sector.
 
• China disputes the legitimacy of the McMahon Line, referring to Arunachal Pradesh as "South Tibet," and this dispute has been a source of tension between the two nations.
 
• The disagreement over the McMahon Line was one of the factors that led to the Sino-Indian War of 1962, during which China captured parts of Arunachal Pradesh but later withdrew.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pakistan**

 
 
• India shares a boundary with Pakistan called the **Radcliffe Line**, which was drawn during the partition of India in 1947.
 
• The India-Pakistan border spans approximately 3,323 kilometers and includes the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir, which is a de facto military boundary.
 
• The Radcliffe Line was named after Sir Cyril Radcliffe, the chairman of the boundary commission, and is distinct from the McMahon Line.
 
 
 
• **Myanmar**
 
 
• India shares a border of about 1,643 kilometers with Myanmar, covering the northeastern states of Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram.
 
• The India-Myanmar boundary is not related to the McMahon Line and was delineated through agreements between the British colonial government and Burma (now Myanmar).
 
• This boundary is significant for trade and cultural exchanges and also for addressing insurgency issues in the northeastern region of India.
 
 
 
• **Afghanistan**
 
 
• India shares a small border with Afghanistan in the northwestern region of Jammu and Kashmir, known as the **Wakhan Corridor**.
 
• This border, approximately 106 kilometers long, lies in the Gilgit-Baltistan region, which is currently under Pakistani control and part of the larger Kashmir dispute.
 
• The boundary was established during the Durand Line agreement of 1893 between British India and Afghanistan, which is unrelated to the McMahon Line.

questions.question: What is the name given to a saucer-shaped intrusive igneous body that is concave to the sky?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lopolith**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A **lopolith** is a saucer-shaped intrusive igneous rock body that has a concave shape facing upwards (towards the sky).
 
• It forms when magma intrudes between layers of sedimentary rock and cools, causing the layers above it to sag.
 
• Lopoliths are typically composed of mafic or ultramafic rocks, such as gabbro or anorthosite.
 
• They are associated with large igneous provinces and are considered important for understanding geological processes of magma emplacement.
 
• Examples of lopoliths include the Bushveld Complex in South Africa, which is one of the largest known lopoliths and a significant source of platinum group elements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sill:**

 
 
• A sill is a flat, horizontal, or nearly horizontal sheet of igneous rock that forms when magma intrudes parallel to the bedding planes of sedimentary rocks.
 
• Sills are concordant intrusions, meaning they do not cut through the layers of rock they intrude.
 
• They differ from lopoliths in their flat shape and lack of sagging caused in the overlying rock layers.
 
 
 
• **Phacolith:**
 
 
• A phacolith is an igneous intrusion that forms in the crests of anticlines or troughs of synclines (geological folds).
 
• It typically has a lens-like or crescent-shaped appearance.
 
• Phacoliths are usually smaller in size compared to lopoliths and are associated with folded sedimentary rocks.
 
 
 
• **Batholith:**
 
 
• A batholith is a large, irregularly shaped mass of intrusive igneous rock that has solidified deep beneath the Earth's surface.
 
• Batholiths are massive and can cover hundreds of square kilometers, often forming the cores of mountain ranges.
 
• An example is the Sierra Nevada Batholith in the western United States.
